analysis.one_liner: Bars EPA for one year from tightening particulate air standards and leaves rural dust regulation mostly to states.
analysis.headline: The House passed the bill 268-150 on December 8, 2011, but the Senate never voted on it and it died when the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have stopped the EPA for one year from revising the national air standard for larger airborne particles, and would have permanently carved "nuisance dust" — dust from farms, unpaved roads, earth moving, and other rural sources — out of the Clean Air Act in areas where state or local law already regulates it. It also required the EPA to produce state-by-state job and economic analyses before any covered dust-related action, and to hold public hearings in any state projected to lose more than 100 agriculture jobs or $1 million in farm economic activity.
analysis.who_benefits: Large farm operations and other rural dust sources — unpaved road operators, earth movers, and agricultural businesses — would avoid federal air-quality costs and oversight, and states would keep primary control over rural dust.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Large farm and rural land operations

how_it_helps.text: The bill exempts nuisance dust from the Clean Air Act everywhere state, tribal, or local law already regulates it, leaving federal regulators out unless the EPA finds substantial health effects and benefits that outweigh costs [S5].
It blocks the EPA for one year from proposing, finalizing, implementing, or enforcing any revision of the national air quality standard for particles larger than 2.5 micrometers [S2].

Before any covered action, the EPA must publish a state-by-state analysis of effects on agricultural jobs and economic activity, and hold a hearing in each state projected to lose more than 100 farm jobs or more than $1 million in agricultural economic activity [S4].
The EPA must notify a state's congressional delegation, governor, and legislature at least 45 days before any covered action takes effect in that state [S5].

analysis.who_pays: People living near and downwind of dust sources — rural residents, farmworkers, children, and people with asthma or heart and lung disease — would bear weaker federal protection from particle pollution, and the EPA would lose a tool for updating health standards when new science shows harm.

drawbacks.text: The bill blocks the EPA from revising a health-based air standard for a full year even if new scientific evidence shows the current standard is too weak to protect public health [S2].

The permanent dust exemption applies wherever state, tribal, or local law regulates dust, even if that regulation is minimal, and the EPA can override it only by finding substantial health effects and benefits that outweigh the costs [S5].

The job-loss trigger — any state losing more than 100 agriculture jobs or $1 million in agricultural economic activity — forces hearings, notices, and delay for actions that affect the whole country's air, because the calculation excludes offsetting gains [S5].

Supporters argued federal farm dust regulation was not actually happening and that the bill solved a problem that did not exist; the carve-outs for combustion exhaust and coal residuals in the final bill show the scope was contested even in committee [S5].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For farm operators the cost savings are real but local: states can already regulate dust, and the bill's definition excludes combustion sources and coal residuals, so the biggest industrial emitters get little relief. For the public, the cost is a one-year freeze on updating a health standard and a permanent federal hands-off rule for rural dust that depends on uneven state enforcement. The bill solves a problem mostly for regulated businesses while shifting health risk to the people who live near the sources.

outcome.mechanism: It passed the House by a wide margin in December 2011, but the Senate never brought it to a vote and it died when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on April 15, 2011, and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee [S7].
The committee reported an amended version on December 6, 2011, after a 33-16 committee vote [S3, S7].
A Democratic motion to recommit the bill with instructions to protect EPA authority over specified emissions failed 166-252, with all 235 voting Republicans opposed [S7, S8].
The House passed the bill 268-150 on December 8, 2011: Republicans voted 235-0 in favor, while Democrats split 33 for and 150 against [S9].
The Senate received the bill on December 12, 2011, and placed it on the calendar, where it remained without a vote through the end of the 112th Congress on January 3, 2013 [S7].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never became law, the EPA kept its existing authority over particulate pollution standards and rural dust, and people living near dust sources kept current federal protections. Farm and rural-industry interests, which had pushed for the exemption, got nothing.

for.name: 235 of 241 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Voted for final passage 235-0 and against the motion to recommit 0-235

for.name: House Committee on Energy and Commerce
for.what_they_did: Marked up and reported the bill amended, 33-16, on December 6, 2011

for.name: American Farm Bureau Federation and allied agricultural groups
for.what_they_did: Ran a public campaign warning that EPA was about to regulate farm dust and pressed Congress to pass the exemption

against.name: 150 of 192 House Democrats
against.what_they_did: Voted against final passage, 150 nays, and for the motion to recommit preserving EPA authority, 166 yeas

against.name: President Obama
against.what_they_did: Issued a statement of administration policy threatening to veto the bill if it reached his desk

against.name: Senate Democratic leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the House-passed bill to a Senate vote before the Congress expired

against.name: Public health organizations, including the American Lung Association
against.what_they_did: Opposed the bill as weakening air-quality protections against particulate pollution

sides.party_line_note: On final passage Republicans voted 235-0 in favor while Democrats opposed 150-33, though the 268-150 total included 33 Democratic votes for the bill.

industries.industry: Agriculture industry and large farm operations
industries.note: The bill would free farm dust from Clean Air Act coverage in most areas and freeze the particulate standard for a year, cutting compliance costs for large operations. The cost falls on nearby rural residents and farmworkers, who breathe the same dust the bill would leave to uneven state enforcement.

industries.industry: Rural road operators, earth moving, and construction
industries.note: The bill's definition of nuisance dust covers dust from unpaved roads, earth moving, and other rural activities, so these operations would get the same federal hands-off treatment. Their emissions settle on the homes and schools of people living nearby.

industries.industry: Combustion-source industries, including coal-burning power plants
industries.note: The final bill explicitly excludes combustion exhaust, coal combustion residuals, and uranium dust from the exemption, so industrial smokestack sources were not handed the same relief as farm and road dust. The one-year freeze on revising the coarse-particle standard gives them a modest benefit.
